patient.chief_complaint: Sudden bilateral leg weakness — unable to walk for 24 hours
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. T is a 22-year-old college senior and pre-medical student who presents with 24 hours of bilateral leg weakness severe enough to prevent ambulation. She reports waking yesterday morning unable to move her legs. She had gone to sleep feeling well after a long study session. She has been a high-achieving student throughout her academic career; however, she failed a major organic chemistry examination 2 weeks ago for the first time, creating significant distress. Her family, who immigrated from West Africa, has invested substantially in her education and she feels immense pressure to succeed and become a physician. She has no prior neurological symptoms. She denies any sensory changes, pain, bowel or bladder dysfunction, fever, or headache. She has not had any recent illness. There is no history of trauma. She has no medications and no substance use. Her roommate reports she has been sleeping poorly and crying frequently since the exam failure. The weakness onset was abrupt, occurring overnight without any prodromal symptoms. She denies any prior similar episodes. She has no family history of neurological disease.

results.title: Functional neurological disorder: updated review with emphasis on diagnosis and treatment
The FND challenge: updating the clinical framework

output.summary: Functional neurological disorder has recognized neurobiological correlates including altered brain connectivity and predictive coding abnormalities in neuroimaging studies. It is distinct from malingering. Evidence-based management includes FND-specific physiotherapy and CBT; treatment outcomes are better with earlier intervention and shorter symptom duration. Family psychoeducation regarding the neurobiological basis of the condition is associated with reduced stigma in cohort studies.

differential.key_features: Anti-AQP4 and MOG-IgG both negative in serum and CSF; MRI spine normal — no cord T2 lesion; important consideration in young Black female
MRI spine normal; CSF normal; no sensory level; no bladder dysfunction
Reflexes normal (GBS causes areflexia); normal NCS (GBS shows slowed conduction); CSF protein normal (GBS shows albumino-cytologic dissociation)
FND is NOT malingering — it is an involuntary neurological disorder with neurobiological basis; should not be labeled as malingering without clear evidence of intentional simulation

optimal_actions.action: MRI brain and full spine — emergent exclusion of cord compression
Labs including anti-AQP4, MOG-IgG, ANA (critical in young Black female)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: All negative — NMO and autoimmune myelitis excluded

optimal_actions.action: EMG and NCS — exclude GBS and neuropathy
Psychiatric evaluation and FND physiotherapy referral
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Depression, anxiety, identified academic stress precipitant

critical_actions: Anti-AQP4 and MOG-IgG — NMOSD exclusion critical in young Black female
Explain FND diagnosis compassionately and explain it is NOT feigning
contraindicated_actions: Accusing patient of malingering or feigning
High-dose steroids without inflammatory myelopathy diagnosis
key_reasoning_points: NMOSD (NMO spectrum disorder) is significantly more prevalent in young Black females — anti-AQP4 and MOG-IgG are critical tests that must be included in the differential
Bilateral Hoover sign demonstrates that corticospinal motor pathways are INTACT — the diagnosis of functional weakness is positive, not merely by exclusion
Normal MUP recruitment on EMG during attempted movement (patient can generate normal signals when not consciously trying) confirms intact lower motor neuron
The speed of recovery with physiotherapy (5 days to full ambulation) confirms functional etiology — organic bilateral paraparesis does not recover this rapidly

metadata.notes: Straightforward FND, bilateral functional paraplegia in young Black female pre-med student. Anti-AQP4 and MOG-IgG critical to check given demographics.
